Short questions to test your understanding of penalized linear models. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** Why does ordinary least squares fail (or become unstable) when you have 20 000 genes and 40 samples?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Count unknowns versus equations.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
There are far more unknown coefficients ($p = 20\,000$, one per gene) than equations ($n = 40$, one per sample), so the system is **underdetermined** — infinitely many coefficient sets fit the training data perfectly, including its noise, and nothing tells ordinary least squares which one to pick. Co-regulated genes make it worse: their coefficients can trade off against each other without changing the fit. This is the $p \gg n$ regime.
:::

---

**Q2.** Describe in words what penalized regression makes as small as possible, and give the penalty sum for ridge and for lasso.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Fit term plus $\lambda$ times a penalty. Squares vs. absolute values.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The **total squared miss** on the training data (how badly the model fits) **plus $\lambda$ times a penalty** for large coefficients; $\lambda$ sets how much the penalty counts.
Ridge (L2): penalty $= \sum_j \beta_j^2$. Lasso (L1): penalty $= \sum_j \lvert\beta_j\rvert$.
:::

---

**Q3.** What is the single most important behavioural difference between ridge and lasso?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to a coefficient that is not useful?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Lasso sets some coefficients exactly to zero** (dropping those predictors — automatic feature selection, a sparse model). **Ridge shrinks all coefficients toward zero but keeps them all nonzero.** So lasso selects; ridge only shrinks.
:::

---

**Q4.** In the constraint-geometry picture, the ridge budget region is a **circle** and the lasso region is a **diamond**. Why does that difference produce zero coefficients for lasso but not for ridge?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where are the corners of the diamond, and what does the RSS ellipse tend to touch first?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The diamond has **corners that lie on the axes**, where one coordinate is exactly zero. The expanding RSS ellipse tends to first touch a pointy **corner**, so the lasso solution often lands with a coefficient exactly $0$. The circle is smooth with no corners, so ridge's touch point sits at a generic location with all coefficients nonzero.
:::

---

**Q5.** Two genes are almost perfectly correlated and both affect the phenotype. Why are the ordinary least squares coefficients unstable, and why is ridge stable?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The data pin down the combined effect of the two genes. What decides the split? What does a sum of squares prefer: one big coefficient or two medium ones?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The two genes carry the same signal, so the data only pin down their **combined** effect; ordinary least squares is free to split it any way (e.g. $5$ and $-3$ instead of $1$ and $1$), and which split it returns is decided by noise — a new dataset gives a very different split. Ridge **shares the weight**: two medium coefficients cost less in $\sum\beta_j^2$ than one big and one negative, so it settles on roughly equal values near the truth every time (in the resampling demo, $\hat\beta_1$ stays between about 0.7 and 1.2 while ordinary least squares ranges from about $-1.8$ to $5.4$).

(Optional, in matrix terms: ridge is $(X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top\mathbf{y}$; adding $\lambda I$ raises every eigenvalue of $X^\top X$ by $\lambda$, so a near-zero eigenvalue becomes at least $\lambda$ and the matrix is safely invertible.)
:::

---

**Q6.** What is the elastic net, and what practical problem with lasso does it fix in genomics?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
It mixes two penalties with a parameter $\alpha$. Think about a group of co-regulated genes.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Elastic net uses a **mix** of L1 and L2: penalty $= \alpha\times$ lasso penalty $+ (1-\alpha)\times$ ridge penalty, with $\alpha=1$ pure lasso and $\alpha=0$ pure ridge. It fixes lasso's tendency to pick **one gene arbitrarily** from a group of correlated (co-regulated) genes and drop the rest: the L2 part encourages correlated genes to be **selected or dropped together** (the grouping effect), giving more stable, biologically sensible selection.
:::

---

**Q7.** How should you choose $\lambda$, and why can you **not** just pick the $\lambda$ that minimizes the training error?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to training error as $\lambda \to 0$? Which model does that favour?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Choose $\lambda$ by **cross-validation** — estimate error on held-out folds and pick the $\lambda$ with the lowest cross-validated error (`lambda.min`, or the sparser `lambda.1se` within one SE). You cannot use training error because it falls monotonically as $\lambda \to 0$, so it would always select the **overfit** ordinary least squares model. Only out-of-sample error reveals the right amount of shrinkage.
:::

---

**Q8.** You run `cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1)` and extract coefficients at `lambda.1se`. Most entries are zero; a few genes are nonzero. In biological terms, what is that short list, and what is one important caveat about it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Selected genes are a signature. Does "selected" mean "causal"?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The nonzero genes are the model's **selected predictive signature** — a short, testable panel that predicts the phenotype and could be turned into a targeted assay. Caveat: these genes are **predictive, not proven causal**. Because of collinearity a dropped gene may be just as relevant as the one kept, and the exact list can shift across CV splits at small $n$. Interpret it as a hypothesis to **validate experimentally**, not as established biology.
:::
